intro.x: A vector field assigns a vector to every point of a region. Wind velocity, water flow, gravity and the electric field are all vector fields. In this chapter we learn to describe how a vector field spreads out (divergence) and how it rotates (curl), and we prove the identities that connect these operators with the gradient.

blocks.x: A vector field on a set $U\subseteq\R^n$ is a map $\vec F:U\to\R^n$. In $\R^3$ we write $\vec F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)=(P,Q,R)$, where each component is a scalar function of $(x,y,z)$.
We draw a field by placing, at many points, an arrow in the direction of $\vec F$ with length proportional to $\norm{\vec F}$.

blocks.caption: Four basic planar vector fields. The radial field has divergence $2$ and curl $0$. The rotation field has divergence $0$ and curl $2\khat$. The saddle flow has divergence $0$ and curl $0$. The shear has divergence $0$ and curl $-\khat$.

blocks.x: A flow line (or integral curve) of $\vec F$ is a curve $\vec r(t)$ with $\vec r\,'(t)=\vec F(\vec r(t))$: a particle that moves with the field. For $\vec F=(-y,x)$ the flow lines are circles, because $\vec r=(\cos t,\sin t)$ satisfies $\vec r\,'=(-\sin t,\cos t)=(-y,x)$.
These fields appear again and again:
Gradient field: $\vec F= abla f$, for example $ abla( frac12 orm{\vec r}^2)=\vec r$.
Position field: $\vec F(\vec r)=\vec r=(x,y,z)$.
Rigid rotation: $\vec F(\vec r)=\vec\omega\times\vec r$ (velocity of a body that rotates with angular velocity $\vec\omega$).
Inverse-square field: $\vec F(\vec r)=\vec r/\norm{\vec r}^3=\rhat/r^2$ (gravity or the electric field of a point charge).
For a differentiable vector field $\vec F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)$ the divergence is the scalar function
\divg\vec F=\pd{F_1}x+\pd{F_2}y+\pd{F_3}z .

The symbol $\nabla=(\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z)$ is a “vector of operators”, and $\divg\vec F$ is read as the formal dot product $\nabla\cdot\vec F$. Divergence has a clear physical meaning, which we now prove.

Let $\vec F$ be $C^1$ near $\vec a$. Let $Q_\eps$ be the cube of side $\eps$ centred at $\vec a$, with faces parallel to the coordinate planes, and let $\Phi_\eps$ be the outward flux of $\vec F$ through the boundary of $Q_\eps$ (the integral over the six faces of $\vec F\cdot\hat{\vec n}$, with $\hat{\vec n}$ the outward unit normal). Then
\divg\vec F(\vec a)=\lim_{\eps\to0}\frac{\Phi_\eps}{\eps^3}.
Write $\vec a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ and $h=\eps/2$. The two faces perpendicular to the $x$-axis are at $x=a_1\pm h$ with outward normals $\pm\ihat$. Their combined flux is
\int_{a_2-h}^{a_2+h}\!\int_{a_3-h}^{a_3+h}\Bigl[F_1(a_1+h,y,z)-F_1(a_1-h,y,z)\Bigr]\dd z\,\dd y .

By the mean value theorem, the bracket equals $2h\,\partial_xF_1(\xi,y,z)=\eps\,\partial_xF_1(\xi,y,z)$ for some $\xi=\xi(y,z)\in(a_1-h,a_1+h)$. Since $\partial_xF_1$ is continuous at $\vec a$, for every $\delta>0$ and small enough $\eps$ we have $\abs{\partial_xF_1(\xi,y,z)-\partial_xF_1(\vec a)}<\delta$ on the face. Hence this flux equals $\eps\cdot\eps^2\bigl(\partial_xF_1(\vec a)+\text{error}\bigr)$ with $\abs{\text{error}}<\delta$. The same argument works for the faces perpendicular to $y$ and $z$. Adding the three pairs,
\Phi_\eps=\eps^3\bigl(\partial_xF_1+\partial_yF_2+\partial_zF_3\bigr)(\vec a)+\eps^3\cdot(\text{error}\to0),
and dividing by $\eps^3$ gives the claim.

blocks.caption: A small box in a field that grows in the $x$-direction. More flux leaves through the right face than enters through the left face, so the net outflow is positive: the divergence is positive.

blocks.x: Think of $\vec F$ as the velocity of a fluid. Then $\divg\vec F$ is the rate at which fluid is created (a source) per unit volume at that point. If $\divg\vec F>0$ the point is a source, if $\divg\vec F<0$ it is a sink, and if $\divg\vec F=0$ the fluid is incompressible there: whatever flows into a tiny box also flows out.
Three computations of divergence:
$\vec F=\vec r=(x,y,z)$: $\divg\vec F=1+1+1=3$.
$\vec F=\vec\omega\times\vec r$ with $\vec\omega=(0,0,\omega)$, so $\vec F=\omega(-y,x,0)$: $\divg\vec F=0+0+0=0$.

The inverse-square field $\vec F=\vec r/r^3$, $r=\norm{\vec r}$, for $\vec r\ne\vec 0$. Using $\partial_xr=x/r$, $\partial_x(x\,r^{-3})=r^{-3}-3x^2r^{-5}$, and similarly for $y,z$. Summing, $\divg\vec F=3r^{-3}-3(x^2+y^2+z^2)r^{-5}=3r^{-3}-3r^{-3}=0$.
The last example is important: away from the origin the inverse-square field has no sources. All the “source” sits at the origin (Chapter 8).
For a differentiable field $\vec F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)$ the curl is the vector field

\curl\vec F=\det\begin{pmatrix}\ihat&\jhat&\khat\\\partial_x&\partial_y&\partial_z\\F_1&F_2&F_3\end{pmatrix}
=\Bigl(\pd{F_3}y-\pd{F_2}z,\ \pd{F_1}z-\pd{F_3}x,\ \pd{F_2}x-\pd{F_1}y\Bigr).
For a planar field $\vec F=(P,Q)$ (with no $z$-dependence and $F_3=0$) only the third component remains: $\curl\vec F=(Q_x-P_y)\,\khat$.

Let $\vec F=(P,Q)$ be a $C^1$ planar field, and let $S_\eps$ be the square of side $\eps$ centred at $\vec a=(a,b)$ with sides parallel to the axes. Let $\Gamma_\eps=\oint_{\partial S_\eps}\vec F\cdot\dd\vec r$ be the circulation of $\vec F$ around $\partial S_\eps$, counterclockwise. Then
\pd Qx(\vec a)-\pd Py(\vec a)=\lim_{\eps\to0}\frac{\Gamma_\eps}{\eps^2}.

Let $h=\eps/2$. Going counterclockwise: along the bottom side ($y=b-h$) the direction is $+\ihat$, along the right side ($x=a+h$) it is $+\jhat$, along the top ($y=b+h$) it is $-\ihat$, and along the left side ($x=a-h$) it is $-\jhat$. So
\Gamma_\eps=\int_{a-h}^{a+h}\!\bigl[P(x,b-h)-P(x,b+h)\bigr]\dd x+\int_{b-h}^{b+h}\!\bigl[Q(a+h,y)-Q(a-h,y)\bigr]\dd y .

By the mean value theorem, $P(x,b-h)-P(x,b+h)=-\eps\,P_y(x,\eta(x))$ and $Q(a+h,y)-Q(a-h,y)=\eps\,Q_x(\xi(y),y)$. Both $P_y$ and $Q_x$ are continuous at $\vec a$, so each integral equals $\eps\cdot\eps\,(\mp P_y(\vec a)\text{ resp. }Q_x(\vec a))+o(\eps^2)$. Thus $\Gamma_\eps=\eps^2(Q_x-P_y)(\vec a)+o(\eps^2)$.

blocks.caption: Circulation around a small square. Counterclockwise flow along the top is not cancelled by the weaker clockwise flow along the bottom, so the net circulation is positive: a small paddle wheel placed here would spin counterclockwise.

blocks.x: Imagine a tiny paddle wheel placed in a flowing fluid. Its axis points along $\curl\vec F$, it spins at angular speed $\tfrac12\norm{\curl\vec F}$ (see the next theorem), and the direction of rotation is given by the right-hand rule. If the curl is $\vec0$ the field is called irrotational.
For a constant vector $\vec\omega$ and $\vec F(\vec r)=\vec\omega\times\vec r$, we have $\curl\vec F=2\vec\omega$ and $\divg\vec F=0$.

The proof is short using index notation, which we introduce next. So the curl of the velocity field of a rotating body is twice its angular velocity; this is the exact meaning of “curl measures local rotation”.
Three computations of curl:
$\vec F=\vec r$: $\curl\vec F=\vec 0$ (each component $\partial_yz-\partial_zy=0$).
$\vec F=(-y,x,0)$: $\curl\vec F=(0,0,\partial_x x-\partial_y(-y))=(0,0,2)$.

The field $\vec G=\dfrac{(-y,x)}{x^2+y^2}$ on $\R^2\setminus\{0\}$. With $P=-y/\rho^2$, $Q=x/\rho^2$, $\rho^2=x^2+y^2$: $Q_x=(y^2-x^2)/\rho^4$ and $P_y=-(x^2-y^2)/\rho^4=(y^2-x^2)/\rho^4$. So $\curl\vec G=\vec 0$ everywhere it is defined. We will see in Chapter 6 that $\vec G$ is nevertheless not a gradient. This is the standard example of the role of topology.
For a $C^2$ scalar function $f$, the Laplacian is
\lap f=\divg(\nabla f)=\pdd fx+\pdd fy+\pdd fz .
For a vector field, $\lap\vec F$ means the Laplacian of each component. A function with $\lap f=0$ is called harmonic.
Let $f$ be $C^2$ near $\vec a\in\R^n$ and let $M_\eps$ denote the average value of $f$ over the sphere of radius $\eps$ centred at $\vec a$. Then
M_\eps=f(\vec a)+\frac{\eps^2}{2n}\,\lap f(\vec a)+o(\eps^2).
By Taylor’s theorem (Theorem 2.20), for $\norm{\vec h}=\eps$,
f(\vec a+\vec h)=f(\vec a)+\nabla f(\vec a)\cdot\vec h+\tfrac12\vec h^{\mathsf T}\Hess f(\vec a)\vec h+o(\eps^2).

Average over the sphere. The average of $\vec h$ is $\vec0$ by symmetry ($\vec h\to-\vec h$). For the quadratic term we need the averages of $h_ih_j$: by the symmetry $h_i\to-h_i$, the average of $h_ih_j$ is $0$ for $i\ne j$; by the symmetry that exchanges coordinates, all $\langle h_i^2\rangle$ are equal; and $\sum_i\langle h_i^2\rangle=\langle\norm{\vec h}^2\rangle=\eps^2$, so $\langle h_i^2\rangle=\eps^2/n$. Hence the average of the quadratic term is $\tfrac12\sum_if_{x_ix_i}\,\eps^2/n=\frac{\eps^2}{2n}\lap f(\vec a)$.

The Laplacian compares the value of $f$ at a point with the average of its neighbours. If $\lap f>0$, $f$ at the point is below the neighbourhood average (like the bottom of a bowl). If $\lap f<0$, it is above (a hill top). If $\lap f=0$, the value equals the average: the mean value property of harmonic functions. This is why heat flows towards lower neighbour-averages and why $\lap$ appears in the heat and wave equations (Chapter 8).
Three harmonic-function computations:

$f=1/r$ in $\R^3$ (for $r\ne0$): $\partial_x(r^{-1})=-x\,r^{-3}$, $\partial_x^2(r^{-1})=-r^{-3}+3x^2r^{-5}$. Summing over $x,y,z$: $\lap(1/r)=-3r^{-3}+3r^{-3}=0$. So $1/r$ is harmonic away from the origin. (It is the potential of the inverse-square field: $\nabla(1/r)=-\vec r/r^3$.)
$f=\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ in $\R^2$ is harmonic away from the origin; check: with $\rho^2=x^2+y^2$ we have $f_x=x/\rho^2$ and $f_{xx}=(y^2-x^2)/\rho^4$, $f_{yy}=(x^2-y^2)/\rho^4$, which sum to $0$.

sections.title: Index notation and a toolbox of identities

blocks.x: Vector identities can be proved by writing everything in components. To avoid long expansions we use two symbols.

$\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. The Levi-Civita symbol $\eps_{ijk}$ ($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) is $+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$ (that is $123$, $231$, $312$), $-1$ if it is odd ($132$, $213$, $321$), and $0$ if two indices are equal.

We use the summation convention: a repeated index is summed over $1,2,3$. For example, $a_ib_i=\vec a\cdot\vec b$ and $\partial_iF_i=\divg\vec F$ (where $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x_i$). Directly from the definitions,
(\vec a\times\vec b)_i=\eps_{ijk}a_jb_k,\qquad(\curl\vec F)_i=\eps_{ijk}\,\partial_jF_k,\qquad\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=\eps_{ijk}a_ib_jc_k .
The Levi-Civita symbol is antisymmetric: swapping two indices changes the sign, and it is invariant under cyclic permutation, $\eps_{ijk}=\eps_{jki}=\eps_{kij}$.
$\eps_{kij}\,\eps_{klm}=\delta_{il}\delta_{jm}-\delta_{im}\delta_{jl}$ (sum over $k$).

For fixed $i,j,l,m$ the sum over $k$ has at most one non-zero term, since $k$ must differ from $i$ and $j$ (for $\eps_{kij}
e0$ we need $i
e j$ and then $k$ is the third index). So the left side is $0$ unless $i
e j$, and similarly unless $l
e m$; and it needs $\{l,m\}=\{i,j\}$ for the same $k$. If $(l,m)=(i,j)$ both symbols are equal, the product is $+1$, and the right side is $\delta_{ii}\delta_{jj}-\delta_{ij}\delta_{ji}=1-0=1$. If $(l,m)=(j,i)$, the second symbol is $\eps_{kji}=-\eps_{kij}$, the product is $-1$, and the right side is $\delta_{ij}\delta_{ji}-\delta_{ii}\delta_{jj}=-1$. In all other cases both sides are $0$.
For $C^2$ scalar fields $f,g$ and $C^2$ vector fields $\vec F,\vec G$:
$\curl(\nabla f)=\vec 0$.
$\divg(\curl\vec F)=0$.

abla(fg)=f

$\divg(f\vec F)=\nabla f\cdot\vec F+f\,\divg\vec F$.
$\curl(f\vec F)=\nabla f\times\vec F+f\,\curl\vec F$.
$\divg(\vec F\times\vec G)=\vec G\cdot(\curl\vec F)-\vec F\cdot(\curl\vec G)$.
$\curl(\curl\vec F)=\nabla(\divg\vec F)-\lap\vec F$.
$\lap(fg)=f\lap g+2\nabla f\cdot\nabla g+g\lap f$.

(1) $[\curl\nabla f]_i=\eps_{ijk}\partial_j\partial_kf$. The symbol $\eps_{ijk}$ is antisymmetric in $(j,k)$, while $\partial_j\partial_kf$ is symmetric in $(j,k)$ by Clairaut’s theorem (Theorem 2.6). A sum of an antisymmetric quantity times a symmetric one is $0$: indeed $S=\eps_{ijk}s_{jk}=\eps_{ikj}s_{kj}=-\eps_{ijk}s_{jk}=-S$ (rename the dummy indices $j\leftrightarrow k$), so $S=0$.
(2) $\divg\curl\vec F=\partial_i(\eps_{ijk}\partial_jF_k)=\eps_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_jF_k=0$, because $\eps_{ijk}$ is antisymmetric in $(i,j)$ and $\partial_i\partial_j$ is symmetric.
(3) This is the one-variable product rule applied to each component.
(4) $\partial_i(fF_i)=(\partial_if)F_i+f\,\partial_iF_i$.
(5) $[\curl(f\vec F)]_i=\eps_{ijk}\partial_j(fF_k)=\eps_{ijk}(\partial_jf)F_k+f\,\eps_{ijk}\partial_jF_k=[\nabla f\times\vec F]_i+f[\curl\vec F]_i$.

(6) $\divg(\vec F\times\vec G)=\partial_i(\eps_{ijk}F_jG_k)=\eps_{ijk}(\partial_iF_j)G_k+\eps_{ijk}F_j(\partial_iG_k)$. In the first term $\eps_{ijk}=\eps_{kij}$, so it equals $G_k\,\eps_{kij}\partial_iF_j=\vec G\cdot\curl\vec F$. In the second term $\eps_{ijk}=-\eps_{jik}$, so it equals $-F_j\,\eps_{jik}\partial_iG_k=-\vec F\cdot\curl\vec G$.
(7) Using $\eps_{ijk}=\eps_{kij}$ and Lemma 3.14,
(8) $\lap(fg)=\partial_i\partial_i(fg)=\partial_i(g\,\partial_if+f\,\partial_ig)=g\lap f+2\,\partial_if\,\partial_ig+f\lap g$.

Also $ abla imes abla f=\vec0$ is not “because a vector crossed with itself is zero”; it is true because mixed partials commute. The identity can fail if $f$ is not $C^2$.

sections.title: Irrotational and conservative fields; the Poincar'e lemma

blocks.x: By identity (1), every gradient field has zero curl. Is the converse true? Locally, yes.

A field $\vec F$ is conservative if $\vec F=\nabla f$ for some scalar function $f$ (the potential; by convention in physics the potential energy is $-f$). It is irrotational if $\curl\vec F=\vec 0$. A set $U\subseteq\R^3$ is star-shaped with respect to $\vec 0$ if for every $\vec x\in U$ the whole segment from $\vec 0$ to $\vec x$ lies in $U$ (balls and boxes are star-shaped).
Let $U\subseteq\R^3$ be open and star-shaped with respect to $\vec 0$, and let $\vec F$ be $C^1$ on $U$ with $\curl\vec F=\vec 0$. Then $\vec F=\nabla f$, where
f(\vec x)=\int_0^1\vec F(t\vec x)\cdot\vec x\,\dd t .

The function $f$ is well defined because $t\vec x\in U$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Since $\vec F$ is $C^1$, we may differentiate under the integral sign (justified in Chapter 4, Theorem 4.14). With $f(\vec x)=\int_0^1F_i(t\vec x)\,x_i\,\dd t$,
\partial_jf=\int_0^1\Bigl[F_j(t\vec x)+t\,x_i\,(\partial_jF_i)(t\vec x)\Bigr]\dd t .
The condition $\curl\vec F=\vec 0$ means $\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j$ for all $i,j$. Therefore
\partial_jf=\int_0^1\Bigl[F_j(t\vec x)+t\,x_i\,(\partial_iF_j)(t\vec x)\Bigr]\dd t=\int_0^1\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\Bigl[t\,F_j(t\vec x)\Bigr]\dd t=F_j(\vec x),
because by the chain rule $\frac{\dd}{\dd t}F_j(t\vec x)=x_i(\partial_iF_j)(t\vec x)$.

The formula for $f$ is a line integral of $\vec F$ along the straight segment from the origin to $\vec x$. The theorem says: in a “hole-free” region, an irrotational field has a potential, found by integrating along any path from a base point. In a region with a hole (like the plane minus the origin) the argument breaks, because the region is not star-shaped; and indeed the field $\vec G=(-y,x)/(x^2+y^2)$ is irrotational but has no potential on $\R^2\setminus\{\vec 0\}$ (Chapter 6).

Find a potential of $\vec F=(2xy+z^2,\ x^2,\ 2xz)$. First check $\curl\vec F=(0-0,\ 2z-2z,\ 2x-2x)=\vec 0$. Integrate $f_x=2xy+z^2$: $f=x^2y+xz^2+c(y,z)$. Then $f_y=x^2+c_y$ must equal $x^2$, so $c_y=0$; and $f_z=2xz+c_z$ must equal $2xz$, so $c_z=0$. Hence $f=x^2y+xz^2$ (plus a constant).

By identity (2), every curl is divergence-free. The converse is also true on suitable regions: if $\divg\vec F=0$ on a ball, then $\vec F=\curl\vec A$ for some vector potential $\vec A$ (Chapter 9). On a region with a cavity this can fail: the inverse-square field $\vec r/r^3$ is divergence-free on $\R^3\setminus\{\vec 0\}$ but is not the curl of any field there, because its flux through a sphere around the origin is $4\pi\ne0$ (Chapter 7). The pattern is clear:
Each arrow followed by the next gives zero. This chain is the three-dimensional vector-calculus version of the de Rham complex, treated in Chapter 10.
$\divg\vec F=\partial_xF_1+\partial_yF_2+\partial_zF_3$: net outflow (source strength) per unit volume.
$\curl\vec F$: local rotation. Circulation per unit area $=(\curl\vec F)\cdot\hat{\vec n}$. For a rigid rotation, $\curl(\vec\omega\times\vec r)=2\vec\omega$.
$\lap f=\divg\nabla f$: value minus neighbourhood average (up to a factor). Harmonic: $\lap f=0$.
$\curl\nabla f=\vec 0$, $\divg\curl\vec F=0$, $\curl\curl\vec F=\nabla\divg\vec F-\lap\vec F$.
Proofs by index notation: $(\vec a\times\vec b)_i=\eps_{ijk}a_jb_k$, and $\eps_{kij}\eps_{klm}=\delta_{il}\delta_{jm}-\delta_{im}\delta_{jl}$.
On star-shaped regions, $\curl\vec F=\vec 0$ implies $\vec F=\nabla f$. Holes can break this.
What does the divergence tell you? Net outflow per unit volume: positive for sources, negative for sinks, zero for incompressible flow.
What does the curl tell you? Local rotation; direction by the right-hand rule; magnitude = twice the angular speed of a paddle wheel.
Why is $\curl\nabla f=\vec 0$? Mixed partial derivatives commute (Clairaut). In components $\eps_{ijk}\partial_j\partial_kf=0$.
Why is $\divg\curl\vec F=0$? The same reason: $\eps_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_jF_k=0$.
Is a curl-free field always a gradient? On star-shaped (more generally simply connected) regions, yes. Not in general: $(-y,x)/(x^2+y^2)$ is the counterexample.
What does $\lap f=0$ mean? The value at every point equals the average of nearby values (mean value property). Examples: $1/r$ in $\R^3$, $\ln r$ in $\R^2$.
Compute $\divg(\vec r/r^3)$. Zero for $\vec r\ne\vec0$, since $3r^{-3}-3r^{-3}=0$.

Compute $\divg$ and $\curl$ of $\vec F=(xy,\,yz,\,zx)$. Is it conservative?
Show that for $f(r)$ depending only on $r=\norm{\vec r}$, $\nabla f=f'(r)\,\rhat$ and $\lap f=f''+\dfrac2rf'$ in $\R^3$. Find all solutions of $\lap f=0$ of this form. (Answer: $f=A+B/r$.)

For $\vec F=\vec\omega\times\vec r$ find the flow lines. For $\vec F=(x,-y)$ find the flow lines (hint: $xy=\text{const}$).
